strengths: The proposed MIDRE is extremely simple, easy to implement, and requires only one hyperparameter, making it practically attractive and potentially complementary to existing defenses.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: 23 setups, 6 model inversion attacks (white-box and label-only), 9 architectures including vision transformers, 3 private datasets, 2 public datasets, and both 64x64 and 224x224 resolutions.

The results consistently show substantial reductions in attack accuracy across many settings while natural accuracy is often only moderately affected; in high-resolution settings, MIDRE even improves natural accuracy over NoDef and baselines, which is a notable empirical finding.
The analysis over random-erasing ratios, masking values, and area ratios provides useful ablations and supports the privacy-utility trade-off claim.
The paper includes qualitative results, KNN-distance evaluations, and a user study, going beyond a single attack-accuracy metric.
The paper honestly discusses broader impacts and limitations, and positions MIDRE as complementary to regularization-based defenses.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited: random erasing is a well-known data augmentation technique, and the contribution is primarily an empirical application of it to MI defense. There is no formal privacy guarantee or deeper theoretical analysis of why or when the defense should work.

The central mechanistic claim that MI attacks require a large amount of private training information encoded in the model is not directly measured or rigorously validated; the evidence is mostly correlational through attack-accuracy curves.

The defense is evaluated only against existing MI attacks that are not adaptive to random erasing. An attacker aware of the defense could potentially adjust the reconstruction objective, so the robustness may be overestimated without adaptive attack experiments.

The user study does not support the claimed improvement: BiDO is selected 153 times versus 147 for MIDRE out of 300 votes, with no statistical significance analysis. This should not be presented as evidence of superiority.

Some reported numbers and captions appear inconsistent or duplicated (e.g., LOMMA+KedMI NoDef attack accuracy is identical for different target architectures, and Table 2 mentions DP while DP results are absent), which weakens confidence in the experimental reporting.
The claim that MIDRE is complementary to existing defenses is not tested; no combined MIDRE+BiDO or MIDRE+MID experiments are provided.

Natural-accuracy differences are sometimes small relative to attack-accuracy variance, and the proposed Δ metric can be inflated by utility loss, so the SOTA trade-off claim is not always statistically established.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: code is said to be in the supplement but is not visible in the manuscript, and the reimplementations of BiDO/MID and attack hyperparameters are not fully detailed in the main text.
The high-resolution natural-accuracy gains over NoDef are surprising and not fully explained; possible differences in training or tuning that could advantage MIDRE are not ruled out.

strengths: The proposed method is extremely simple, adds no conflicting regularization to the training objective, requires only one hyperparameter, and is trivially compatible with existing pipelines — a practical advantage over BiDO/MID which need expensive grid search.

The empirical scope is genuinely large: 23 setups spanning 6 MI attacks (including white-box and label-only), 9 architectures (including a ViT), 5 datasets, and both 64×64 and 224×224 resolutions, with an accompanying analysis section and user study.

The privacy–utility analysis in Sec. 2.2 (varying the RE ratio ae across six diverse setups) is a reasonable way to expose the trade-off curve and shows a consistent pattern that attack accuracy falls faster than natural accuracy.
The ablation studies on masking value and area ratio (Tables 6, 7) are sensible and support the chosen configuration.
weaknesses: Limited originality. Random Erasing is a well-known augmentation (Zhong et al., 2020); the contribution is essentially applying it during training and observing its effect on MI. The claimed "novel insight" is largely the observation that masking reduces recoverable information, which is intuitive and not deeply developed. No comparison against other data-level interventions (Cutout, stronger augmentation, noising) is provided to show RE is special rather than a generic degradation.

The central claim is not well grounded theoretically. The paper repeatedly asserts that RE reduces "private information encoded in the model," but never formalizes or measures this quantity; the mechanism for why masking specifically hurts MI reconstruction more than natural accuracy is only explained post-hoc via GRADCAM "partial-evidence" reasoning (Sec. B.2), which is speculative.

The user study undercuts the main results. The automated attack accuracy gap between MIDRE and BiDO is huge (e.g., PLGMI/VGG16/CelebA: 66.60 vs 92.40, Table 2), yet human voters chose MIDRE's reconstructions as more similar to the private image 147/300 times vs BiDO's 153/300 — statistically indistinguishable. This is precisely the setup used in the user study, so the result suggests the primary attack-accuracy metric substantially overstates the privacy gain, or that the metric and human judgment disagree. The paper instead claims the user study "suggest[s] improved defense performance," which is an overstatement of an inconclusive (and arguably contradictory) result.

Comparison paradigms are inconsistent and fairness of baselines is questionable. Table 2 forces all defenses to the same natural accuracy (79.85 for both BiDO and MIDRE) to compare attack accuracy, whereas Tables 3 and 5 report each method at its own natural accuracy. The reimplementation and "careful tuning" of BiDO and MID are not described (no search ranges, criteria, or operating points), making it hard to tell whether the large attack-accuracy gaps reflect the method or the tuning.

The claim that MIDRE improves natural accuracy over NoDef at 224×224 (e.g., 97.28 vs 94.22, Table 3) is surprising and essentially unexplained; it is at least as likely an artifact of training schedule/hyperparameters used for the NoDef baseline as a genuine benefit of the defense. Similarly, the assertion that RE is "complementary to existing defense methods" is stated but never demonstrated by combining it with MID.

Some empirical details necessary for reproducibility are missing or relegated to the supplement without sufficient concreteness: the evaluation model used as "human proxy" is described only generically (its architecture/training are not specified), attack hyperparameters are said to "follow prior work," and the paper states the method slightly affects natural accuracy while some setups show 6–7% drops, which tempers the "moderately affected" framing.

Presentation and framing have issues: the abstract/intro/conclusion claim "SOTA performance" and being "the first to achieve competitive MI robustness without sacrificing natural accuracy" despite the above inconsistencies; there are typographical errors ("guaranting," "demonstrably"), the main tables are split awkwardly across pages, and the conclusion largely restates claims rather than synthesizing evidence.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and practically useful: repurposing Random Erasing—a known occlusion data-augmentation technique—as a training-time defense against model inversion. The method requires only a single hyperparameter (a_h = 0.4, held constant across all setups), making it trivially reproducible and easy to adopt or combine with existing regularizer-based defenses (BiDO, MID).

The experimental scope is genuinely strong: 23 setups spanning 6 SOTA MI attacks (white-box and label-only), 9 architectures including a vision transformer (MaxViT), 5 datasets, and both 64x64 and 224x224 resolutions, plus a user study. This is broader than most prior MI-defense evaluations and supports the generality claims.

The analysis in Sec. 2.2 (Fig. 2) is clean and directly supports the central trade-off claim, showing attack accuracy collapsing much faster than natural accuracy across all six setups (e.g., Setup 6: 72.69% attack-accuracy drop vs. 0.45% natural-accuracy drop).

The high-resolution results (Tab. 3, Tab. 5) are notable: unlike BiDO/MID, MIDRE often improves natural accuracy over NoDef (up to +3.06%) while still substantially lowering attack accuracy, which is a strong privacy-utility result and worth reporting.

The paper is generally well-written and the algorithm/implementation are described clearly enough to reproduce; compute resources and hyperparameter settings for attacks are documented, and code is claimed in the supplement.
weaknesses: The central mechanism claim—that RE actually reduces private information encoded in the model—is supported only empirically. Much of the reduced 'attack accuracy' is attributed (in the GRADCAM ablation) to the model assigning high likelihood from partial cues, producing false positives on reconstructed images rather than genuinely degrading identity content. This means the reported attack-accuracy drop may partially reflect a metric confound rather than true privacy gain.

The user study (Tab. A.4) shows essentially a tie between MIDRE (147) and BiDO (153) in how often humans judge the reconstruction as resembling the private identity. This is a null result that conflicts with the strong claim of 'substantial degradation in MI reconstruction quality,' and it is presented as evidence of 'improved defense performance' without acknowledging the tension. If human-perceived identity leakage is comparable to BiDO, the practical privacy benefit is overstated.

Originality is moderate: Random Erasing is an established technique, and the contribution is essentially its application to a new problem rather than a fundamentally new defense mechanism or theoretical insight. The 'new insight' (MI needs substantial encoded private information) is intuitive and largely taken as given rather than formalized (e.g., no information-theoretic bound or mutual-information argument linking masking to leakage).

The custom trade-off metric Δ = (AttAcc_NoDef − AttAcc_def)/ (Acc_NoDef − Acc_def) is non-standard and unstable: when the defended model has higher natural accuracy than NoDef (as in several 224x224 rows), the denominator goes negative, yielding a non-sensical or undefined ranking. Relying on Δ as a headline ranking metric (Tabs. 6-7) is questionable; standard metrics should be privileged.

The claim that natural accuracy is 'only moderately affected' is not uniformly true—several 64x64 setups show ~6-7% drops (e.g., VGG16, IR152, FaceNet64 in Tab. 2/4). This is a non-trivial utility cost for face recognition and should be framed more carefully. Also, the fixed a_h=0.4 is chosen from a single ablation setup (PLGMI/FaceNet64), so its optimality across the other 22 setups is not verified.

Some fairness/comparability concerns: BiDO and MID were re-implemented and 'carefully tuned' by the authors, and no hyperparameter search details or sensitivity quantification are given, so it is hard to assess whether the baselines were given comparable tuning effort to MIDRE. No statistical significance testing accompanies the reported differences.

strengths: Novel and useful framing: Random Erasing is a well-known augmentation, and repurposing it as a data-centric MI defense is simple, has no inference cost, and is shown to be complementary to existing objective/architecture-based defenses (MIDRE+NLS, MIDRE+BiDO substantially improve over either alone).

Empirical breadth is a major strength: 37 setups spanning 9 MI attacks (white-box, black-box, label-only), 11 architectures (including ViT/MaxViT), 6 datasets, and multiple resolutions, plus qualitative reconstructions and a user study. Results consistently show large attack-accuracy reductions with small utility cost, often outperforming BiDO, NLS, TL-DMI, and MI-RAD variants.
Multi-faceted evaluation using standard MI metrics (attack accuracy, natural accuracy, KNN distance, delta_eval, delta_face) reinforces the main claim and makes results comparable to prior work.

The feature-space analysis offers a plausible and intuitive mechanism: reconstructed features align with the RE-training features rather than clean private features, and ablations (Partial Erasure vs. Entire Erasing, Random vs. Fixed erasing) support the proposed properties.

Reproducibility is strong: detailed hyperparameters, dataset splits, evaluation models, compute resources, and available code; limitations and broader impacts are discussed honestly rather than avoided.
Ablation studies of masking strategy, masking value, area ratio, aspect ratio, inpainting, and adaptive attacks support the design choices and add confidence in the method's behavior.
weaknesses: The central 'no decrease in utility' claim needs stronger controls. MIDRE models sometimes exceed NoDef natural accuracy (e.g., ResNet18 97.28 vs 94.22; ResNet152 95.47 vs 95.43), which suggests NoDef may be undertrained/unaugmented; the win is partly RE acting as a beneficial regularizer. Comparisons should be at matched utility or against baselines trained with comparable augmentation; only Table 4 partially addresses this.

The feature-space analysis is purely qualitative (2D PCA projections and convex hulls) with no quantitative discrepancy metric. Convex-hull overlap in 2D can be misleading, so the mechanistic claim (Property P1) is illustrative rather than rigorously established.

Adaptive-attack analysis is thin: only two setups and a limited adaptive design, yet the paper concludes that adaptive attacks 'fail to enhance attack performance.' For a defense paper the privacy claim rests heavily on stronger adaptive attacks, so this conclusion is not fully substantiated.

Some headline claims are oversold and internally inconsistent: results show substantial utility drops in several 64x64 setups, and the paper cites '37 setups / 9 attacks' in one place and '34 setups / 7 attacks' in another (Discussion E), indicating sloppiness in reporting.

The user study for high resolution is essentially a tie with TL-DMI (537 vs 509, with 522 'both'), and uses only 3 raters per image; the low-res comparison vs BiDO is more favorable but the study is underpowered and its protocol/metric is ambiguously described.
The trade-off metric delta can produce misleading values (e.g., 712.29, 237.00) when the denominator approaches zero or is negative, and the 'OP' handling is not clearly interpretable.
Presentation issues: frequent typos ('achives', 'trade-of', 'demonstrably'), a hard-to-parse Table 2, and occasionally ambiguous figure/table captions, which reduce clarity.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: defending against model inversion attacks, which pose significant privacy risks, especially for models trained on sensitive data like faces.
The empirical scope is broad, covering 9 MI attack types, 11 architectures, multiple datasets, and varying resolutions, which demonstrates considerable effort in benchmarking.
The proposed defense (MIDRE) is simple, computationally inexpensive, and can be integrated as a plug-in with existing defenses like BiDO and NLS, showing potential for practical adoption.
The paper includes ablation studies (masking value, area ratio, aspect ratio, alternative masking strategies) and an adaptive attack section, which are good practices for MI defense evaluation.
The idea of using a standard data augmentation technique (Random Erasing) as a defense mechanism is novel and could inspire further research into data-centric privacy protections.
The paper provides code and detailed hyperparameter settings, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim relies on a feature-space analysis that is essentially a qualitative visualization using PCA-reduced penultimate layer activations for three identities (Figure 3 and C.5). The authors draw strong causal conclusions from a handful of points and convex hulls without any quantitative metrics or statistical tests. This visual evidence is insufficient to support the broad claim that the method inherently creates a discrepancy between MI-reconstructed and private features.

The 'NoDef' baseline for high-resolution experiments appears to be severely undertrained. The paper reports NoDef natural accuracy around 94-95%, whereas PPA's original paper (Struppek et al., 2022) reports NoDef accuracy around 97-99%. This suspiciously low baseline makes MIDRE's reported improvements look much larger than they are. A fair comparison requires matching the training schedule of the baseline to the defense.

The justification for the 'first to achieve significant degradation in attack accuracy without decrease in utility' claim is not adequately supported. The modest accuracy gains (<3%) on high-resolution setups are likely within noise or due to an underperforming baseline, rather than a clear 'privacy free lunch.' This undermines a major selling point of the paper.

The adaptive attack evaluation is insufficient. The paper only considers attacks where the adversary knows the masking area but not the specific positions, and concludes that MIDRE is robust. A true white-box adaptive attack should account for the random erasure mechanism itself (e.g., by optimizing the inversion objective over multiple random masks or using expectation over transformation techniques), which is standard for evaluating robustness of randomized defenses. Failing to do so leaves the defense's security claim unverified.

The paper is poorly written and organized. Key details (e.g., the exact training setup, how the NoDef baseline was trained for high-resolution datasets) are relegated to the appendix or omitted entirely. The '37 setups' are not clearly enumerated, and the main text jumps between claims without sufficient explanation. The writing needs substantial improvement for clarity.

The presentation of results is sometimes misleading or unclear. For instance, the abstract mentions 'degrade in attack accuracy without decrease in utility,' but the claim in the introduction that MIDRE 'achieves higher natural accuracy but lower attack accuracy than no defense model for larger image sizes (224x224)' is only true for ResNet18 and ResNet152 in Table B.9, not for MaxVIT or other architectures where NoDef is stronger.

The paper lacks a proper statistical analysis. Given only 37 setups, reporting mean and standard deviation across multiple runs or conducting paired tests to assert 'state-of-the-art' would be more rigorous. The standard deviations shown in tables are surprisingly large, yet the authors do not discuss this or its impact on conclusions.

The user study results are counterintuitive and not well explained. In the high-resolution setup (Table B.12), roughly equal numbers of users chose MIDRE (509) and TL-DMI (537) as more similar to private data, and a large majority (522) voted 'both' as similar. This does not clearly support the claim that MIDRE provides superior privacy; if anything, it suggests that both defenses produce images that are similarly recognizable as the private identities, raising questions about the practical privacy benefit.

The limitations section is shallow and does not engage with the major weaknesses of the work (e.g., the suspicious baseline, the weak feature-space analysis, the incomplete adaptive attacks). Addressing these would be necessary for publication.

strengths: The proposed MIDRE method is simple, practical, and easy to integrate: it requires only one hyperparameter and no changes to model architecture or training loss, making it complementary to existing MI defenses.

The evaluation is extensive: 37 experimental setups, 9 SOTA MI attacks including white-box, black-box, and label-only attacks, 11 model architectures including vision transformers, 6 datasets/resolutions, and a user study, with comparisons against NoDef, BiDO, NLS, TL-DMI, MI-RAD, and others.

The feature-space analysis provides a useful explanation for why Random Erasing degrades MI attacks: reconstructed features align with RE-private training features rather than private-image features, creating a mismatch between f_recon and f_priv while private features remain separable enough to preserve utility.

The paper includes informative ablations and analyses of the two key properties of Random Erasing (partial erasure and random location), adaptive attacks, alternative masking strategies, inpainting, masking values, area ratio, and aspect ratio.

Reproducibility is reasonably strong: code and additional results are provided, the supplement gives detailed experimental settings, hyperparameters, datasets, evaluation metrics, and limitations are discussed.
weaknesses: The core technique is not fundamentally new: Random Erasing is a well-known data augmentation, and the contribution is primarily its application and analysis as an MI defense rather than a new privacy mechanism. The paper would benefit from a clearer statement of what is conceptually novel beyond applying an existing augmentation.

Some central claims are over-stated or depend heavily on specific configurations. For example, the claim of achieving significant attack degradation without utility loss is true only for certain high-resolution setups, and the natural-accuracy increase may stem from RE's regularization/generalization effect rather than from privacy-specific behavior.

The adaptive attack evaluation is limited: the attacker is assumed to know the erasure area portions but not more sophisticated aspects of MIDRE, such as position distributions or the ability to simulate RE during inversion more faithfully. Stronger adaptive attacks could potentially recover some inversion quality.

Presentation quality has several issues, including typos, inconsistent numerical statements (e.g., attack accuracy 'decreasing from 15.47% to 39.93%' is unclear/contradictory), and occasional awkward phrasing ('archives', 'trade-of'), which makes some claims harder to verify.

Comparison with some SOTA defenses is incomplete or uneven: several values are marked NA, the PLGMI low-resolution improvement over NLS is modest, and the high-resolution user study against TL-DMI is close (509 vs 537 votes), which weakens the strong 'significantly better' claim.

The paper does not fully explore failure modes or worst-case behavior, such as how sensitive the defense is to a_h at different resolutions, whether an attacker with knowledge of the RE distribution can adapt more effectively, or how MIDRE behaves when the private data distribution differs substantially from the public evaluation data.
